newsitem.title: USA: Maine lawmakers face budget crunch.
newsitem.headline: Maine lawmakers face budget crunch.

text.p: Maine's 118th Legislature prepared for its first gathering Wednesday with a projected $438 million budget shortfall and Gov. Angus King indicating he will support the repeal or deferral of scheduled tax cuts.

The fate of the $372 million in tax cuts -- which lawmakers approved to take effect July 1, 1997, but did not match with spending cuts -- will likely dominate legislative debate through the session, according to political observers.

"Essentially everything is on the table. It is clear, or becoming clear, that it is highly unlikely we're going to be able to close the gap without a combination of tax cut deferrals and (spending) cuts," King's spokesman Dennis Bailey told Reuters.
Lawmakers will concentrate Wednesday on electing new leadership and constitutional officers. The regular session will begin in January.

King has not released specific proposals for addressing the projected budget shortfall, but aides have indicated he will likely use a formula of proposing $2 in spending cuts for every $1 in tax cut deferrals or repeals.

The tax cuts scheduled to take effect July 1 include $180 million in taxes on hospitals, $54.7 million on nursing home, $26.9 million on business machinery and a cap on income tax collections that will reduce revenues by an estimated $110.6 million.

The hospital tax was originally enacted as budget tool to tap matching Medicaid dollars. The King administration has warned that an additional $540 million in federal funding could be lost if the state tax dollars are not replaced.
The state would face a $65.9 million budget shortfall if all of the tax cuts were repealed, according to administrative and legislative estimates.

King, who initially opposed the cuts proposed by Republicans in the Senate, could have an easier time winning their deferral or repeal because Democrats who opposed their enactment won control of the Legislature in November.
"It's a different scene," said Bailey. "We're all ears, if somebody can find a way to close this gap without deferring the tax cuts we'd be happy to listen to them."

Senate Republicans have indicated they will draft a tax reform package that will retain the tax breaks. "I think we did the right thing getting rid of these things," Sen. Peter Mills, told the Portland Press Herald.
Democrats who control the House and Senate Wedesday are expected to elect Mark Lawrence of Kittery to be Senate President and Elizabeth Mitchell of Vassalboro as House Speaker.

Other issues expected to face lawmakers next year include; deregulation of electric utilities, overhaul of the state welfare system, the closure a large mental health institute and the formula for distributing state aid to education.
